cause: Fewer people come to the market when it rains, so {name} sells fewer {item}.
When it rains, customers stay home and the {item} spoil before {name} can sell them, so she loses money on unsold stock.
action: {name} can buy fewer {item} on days when rain is forecast.
{name} can check the weather each morning, buy smaller stock on rainy days, and take WhatsApp orders so regular customers can still buy.
numbers: If she sells 4 fewer baskets at {price}, she loses ₦2,000 that day.
Buying 6 baskets instead of 10 on a rainy day means less waste, so even selling at {price} she keeps more profit than throwing away 4 spoiled baskets.
tools: {name} should be careful with money.
{name} can keep a record of how many {item} sell on rainy and dry days.
{name} can track sales in a notebook, keep an emergency fund for slow days, and compare the record each month to plan stock.

cause: {name} spends small amounts every day without tracking them, so the money from {job} disappears.
{name} has no plan for the {wage} each week, so small daily spending on snacks and data uses it all before month end.
action: {name} can put some money aside on the day she is paid.
On payday {name} can put money in a separate savings box or a mobile wallet first, then plan spending for the rest of the week.
numbers: Saving ₦1,000 from {wage} each week gives ₦4,000 in a month.
If {name} saves ₦1,000 of {wage} weekly, that is ₦4,000 a month, and cutting ₦200 a day on snacks would add about ₦6,000 more.
tools: {name} needs to save.
{name} can make a budget that splits the money into needs, wants and savings.
Using the 50:30:20 rule, {name} can pay herself first on payday, put the savings in an emergency fund, and track every expense.

cause: The ingredients cost more, so {name} makes less profit on each {snack}.
Flour and oil now cost more, so at {snackPrice} each {name} may be selling {snack} for almost what it costs to make.
action: {name} should change something about the price.
{name} can raise the price a little or make each {snack} slightly smaller.
{name} can buy flour and oil in bulk with another seller to get a better price, and tell regular customers early before a small price rise.
numbers: If each {snack} now costs ₦40 to make, selling at {snackPrice} leaves only ₦10 profit.
Costs went from ₦30 to ₦40, so profit fell from ₦20 to ₦10; selling at ₦60 brings profit back to ₦20 per {snack}.
tools: {name} should look at the business.
{name} can work out the profit on each {snack} by taking away the cost from the price.
{name} can record income and expenses each week, compare suppliers, and use the profit figure to set a new budget.

cause: The friend wants back more than {name} borrowed, so the loan has a high cost.
{name} must repay {repay} for a {loan} loan in one month, which is a very high cost, and if sales are slow she could fall into debt.
action: {name} should only take it if she is sure she can sell enough to repay.
{name} should work out expected sales first, ask for a smaller loan or longer time, or save for a few weeks instead.
numbers: She will pay back more money.
She pays back {repay} for {loan}, which is ₦10,000 extra.
Paying ₦10,000 extra on {loan} in one month is 50% interest, so the new stock must make more than ₦10,000 profit just to break even.
tools: Loans need care.
This looks like predatory lending because the interest is so high.
{name} should compare the interest with a cooperative or esusu, check it fits her budget, and save first if the cost is too high.

understanding: {employer} wants a {role} who is reliable and good with customers.
{employer} will want to see that {name} is on time, friendly with customers and can handle money carefully as a {role}.
steps: {name} can choose clean clothes tonight and plan the route to arrive early.
First, {name} can learn what {employer} sells; then practise answers with a friend; finally, prepare clothes and leave 30 minutes early.
communication: {name} should greet the interviewer politely and say thank you.
{name} can say, 'Good morning, thank you for inviting me. I am excited to work with your customers.'
tools: {name} should know about the job.
{name} can research {employer} online and read the job post again.
{name} can research {employer}, use the STAR method (situation, task, action, result) for the problem question, and prepare two questions to ask.

understanding: The manager at {employer} expects {name} on time and will worry if she does not come.
On the first day, the manager at {employer} is planning the shift, so being late without warning looks unreliable.
steps: {name} should call or text the manager before the start time.
First, {name} should message the manager now; then share the arrival time; finally, apologise in person and plan to leave earlier tomorrow.
communication: {name} should politely explain the traffic and apologise.
{name} can text, 'Good morning sir, I am sorry, I am stuck in traffic and will arrive by 8:30. I will leave earlier from tomorrow.'
tools: {name} should think about work rules.
{name} should send a professional message so the manager knows early.
{name} should send a professional message now, follow up when she arrives, and plan to be punctual tomorrow to fix the first impression.

understanding: The customer is upset because they did not get what they paid for.
The customer paid for something and got the wrong thing, so they want the problem fixed quickly and to feel respected.
steps: {name} should check the order and replace the wrong item.
First, {name} should listen without arguing; then check the receipt; finally, replace the item or call the manager if needed.
communication: {name} should stay calm and apologise to the customer.
{name} can say, 'I am very sorry about this. Let me fix your order for you right now.'
tools: {name} should handle it.
{name} can use active listening: let the customer finish and repeat the problem back.
{name} can use active listening and empathy, apologise, fix the order, and follow up so the customer leaves happy.

understanding: Real employers do not ask people to pay to apply, so this may be a scam.
Asking {fee} to apply is a common scam sign; real employers like {employer} do not charge applicants.
steps: {name} should not pay and should check with {employer} directly.
First, {name} should not send money; then visit or call {employer} to check; finally, warn friends and report the advert.
communication: {name} should politely ask {employer} if the advert is real.
{name} can ask, 'Good afternoon, I saw a {role} advert asking for {fee}. Is this from your company?'
tools: {name} should be careful online.
Asking for money to apply is a sign of a scam.
{name} should verify the job on {employer}'s official website, never pay a fee, and report the post as a scam.

diagnosis: The panel could be dirty or in shade, so it does not make enough power to charge the battery.
If a cable is loose no power reaches the battery, and if the battery is old it cannot hold the charge, so the light stays off at night.
tools: I would check the fuse.
I would check the panel output with a multimeter.
I would check the fuse, measure the panel voltage with a multimeter in sunlight, and measure the battery voltage.
order: I would try to fix it.
First I would check the cables are tight.
First I would switch it off and check the cables, then look at the panel in the sun, and finally check the battery.
